Hey Breck, nice to hear from you!
This is something we've talked about at times here at YC. I think Sam was seriously considering it around 2017, including possibly using a crypto token to decrease some of the administrative headache (not clear to me that this would have worked -- I suspect that we'd still have to send out
hundreds of K-1s to all the founders every year, even if the final payouts happened on a blockchain).
I do think it's intriguing, and might talk to Jon about it at some point. He probably has more context on why we didn't decide to go through with it at the time.
If you were joining an equity swap with a startup today, how much equity would you theoretically be willing to give to the common pool?
On Tue, Feb 9, 2021 at 6:14 AM Breck Yunits <breck7@gmail.com> wrote:
Aloha Kyle,
Crazy idea.
The one potential way I could see YC being disrupted is
if some accelerator were to nail the equity swap model.
ie, if there are 10 companies in your batch, each company
gets ~ 1% of the other 9.
Looking back at my 2 YC batches, it seems like it may
turn out to be obvious long run that this would be a
better model for founders. The only downside I could
think of is that somehow it has the unintended 2nd
order effect of lowering the gross value of the batch (
maybe because of excessive free rider problem). But
I could see it going the other way just as likely, in that
not only does it become a better deal for 100% of founders,
but the absolute value of the batches go up as well.
I talked to Jon Levy about this a bit, and he's said that
a few people have tried, but no one has pulled this off.
He thinks the legal challenges are a bit difficult, but I
think that could be done with software. He also intro'd
me to PandoPooling, who I will be talking with this week.
Have you thought about attempting something like this
for SUS?
It could be a worthwhile experiment. You could maybe
do something like take the top 30 companies that just
missed the cutoff for YC, and asked "do you want to
be in one of 3 equity swap batches?"
Okay that's the crazy idea of the day. Hope all is well!
-Breck

There have been a bunch of high profile startup failures lately. This week's casualty, Zirtual, reminded me how crucial it is not to
assume raising more money will be as easy as it was the first time. One article, in particular, had a sentence that literally made
my hair stand on end:

additional money is a "given" and 3) do not be in denial about points 1 and 2.

title: We Don't Negotiate with Terrorists
transcript:
[ycfounders] Fraud

Daniel Sugarman <dsugarman@zentail.com> Thu, Sep 11, 2014 at 7:07 AM
Reply-To: dsugarman@hdtradeservices.com
To: ycfounders@googlegroups.com

Thank you everyone who followed up: David Cann, Tom Sparks, Doug Feigelson, Zaid Farooqui, Benjamin Bryant, Russell Smith, Charlie Pinto, Daniel Conrad, Simon Tisminezky, Kai Stinchcombe, Jesse Cooke, Eric
Migicovsky (& James Pierson @ pebble). Thanks especially to Jason Tan and Patrick Collison for speaking to me on the phone so I can better understand your services. | wanted to put together a basic guide to our findings, |
hope people find this useful. tidr: manually approve any and all orders.

Fraud & Me (as a startup merchant)

The issue of fraud can be quite serious as a startup merchant, especially selling physical products. Your supplier isn't going to eat the cost, neither will the credit card companies which leaves all the liability on you. If you aren't
careful, you will not find out about these issues until the customer issues a chargeback with their credit card companies. This means that you may be selling products for 4+ weeks before you find out you have a problem. A
'company with low margins, like ours, could lose a month of runway a day and wind up out of business by the time the problem is identified.

How to fight fraud

It is important to keep a close eye on your transactions. There is a fine line between providing excellent service to your good customers and preventing bad behaviour. There doesn't seem to be a better solution than to manually
approve every single order at first, and automate more and more as you collect data. The key data points you want to look for are:

Billing Address
Shipping Address

Billing Phone Number
Shipping Phone Number
IP Address (geolocated)
Card Type

Order Size ($ & Quantity)

Most fraud we see is different billing & shipping addresses. The best review process seems to be googling street addresses, checking white page results (or safecaller.com) on the phone numbers and calling the phone
numbers. If you aren't sure, you have a decision to make whether you want to side towards customer service or fraud prevention and that might likely be a calculation with respect to the order size, frequency of fraud and your
runway. | am told that verifying billing phone numbers is impossible, otherwise it would be simple to verify a phone number and then hold the package until you receive a response from the customer.

Friendly" Fraud

Defined as a customer who buys a product and later files a chargeback claim. Make sure that your company name appropriately represents you on your customer's credit card statement. The more data you keep track of, the
easier it will be to win one of these claims. If you use Stripe, they will actually eat the cost of the chargeback claim even though they are charged regardless. To win a claim, provide the IP address, carrier and tracking info as
well as proof of delivery. If you have it, any engagement with support, discovery, registration and shopping cart should be included.

Sift Science

You should definitely use Sift Science, but itis important to really understand their product, they likely won't protect you very much in the beginning. We use their magento plugin and originally wrongfully assumed that they would
automatically prevent orders going through that were fraudulent, this is NOT the case. They provide a machine learning algorithm that will learn your specific attackers pattems as well as more global fraud trends. Their magento
plugin will never prevent an order. The Sift Science global model (data collected from all of their users) will likely not be sufficient in catching your fraud attempts. This means that you must see a number of attacks before the
model leams what attributes are likely to identify a fraudulent attack. If you have repeated attacks of a certain type, the system will become hypersensitive to your attackers. It will also become hypersensitive to vulnerabilities
specific to your platform and customers. It is very important that you manually label fraudulent orders on your dashboard or the system will never learn.

Stripe

You all know and love Stripe, they lead the space in ease of connectivity for developers. Stripe is also great for chargebacks because they will pay the fee if you win a claim (normally you are charged either way). Stripe might
lead you to a catch 22, do you store credit card info or not. With this info, you are strongly liable. Without it, it will be very hard to troubleshoot to a certain degree; it will be downright impossible (without custom work*) to contact
the issuing bank to find out more information or to provide the FBI with the information they request. Stripe does not currently provide phone support, do not expect to get enough information from their email support to make a
decision on intercepting a package. The issue is that there really isn't much they can do on a complex attack and the time window is so small, just intercept the package. If you can, hold off on shipping any suspicious order.
I would email patrick@stripe.com right away if you have any major problems, he is very responsive and deeply wants to help YC companies (he even offered custom work if that was the diagnosis).

"Itis possible to use Stripe's API to get the issuing bank information. You can be proactive and record this information on every order and contact the bank where necessary. | am told these inquiries don't generally go far.

Loo! ito (help if you can!)

'Our Attack

We have seen a diverse set of attacks from friendly to really technically advanced. Some were easy to detect, ex. IP from foreign address and shipping to a freight forwarder. Our biggest attack was really hard to detect. Our
attackers used stolen credit card information to send packages to residential addresses close to the credit card holder. They would also use a proxy to access our website close to the shipping and billing addresses. They would
list the billing and shipping phone to be the same phone number and these numbers would be from the correct area as our "customer". Without verification on the billing phone #, we didn't know if these #s are real or fake.
Thankfully all of these phone numbers went to the same 2 people.

Select Raw Responses

'Tom Sparks - Sounds like you could use IPViking, its a live list of attackers/fraudsters. If you've got a list of the IP's from the folks who've ripped you off, I'l run it against the list and see how many of them would've been caught.

Charlie Pinto - This is what happens when you deal with payments. The best course of action would be to store the cards yourselves, save as much contextual data as you can (geo-location, information, card type, amount,

Mon, Feb 3, 2014, 12:55 PM
:
The YC founders list is a super valuable resource, but as it grows, we have to make sure it continues to be valuable. With this many people, it has to be a moderated list.
There's one rule to posts that get sent out:
Would the majority of people on this list get some sort of benefit by seeing this thread and its replies?
A few quick guidelines:
• If you're relatively new to the list, please use search first to see if it's been asked. https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/ycfounders
• Questions like "How do I do X?" are welcome. Polling for knowledge and compiling responses is always helpful.
• Questions like "Does anyone know X person, company, or vendor?" are also appropriate, with caveats. If this is an urgent or important request, e.g. servers are down, or something material
to your business, by all means. It is best to start with your specific batch's list first. Don't post trivial introduction requests.
• Candidate recommendations are welcome only if you have personally worked with the person or are close personal friends and are willing to vouch for them. It's not OK if they're a random
friend's / brother's / barber's neighbor, or you wouldn't hire them yourself.
A few don'ts:
• Don't post hiring notices / job posts. Everyone's also hiring.
• Don't post launch press. Everyone is also launching things.
• Don't post blind requests from other companies or non-YC people. It's inappropriate to ask if anyone wants to meet your investor or advisor, or promote outside needs that would not meet the
one bold rule mentioned above.
• Don't post events, unless you or your company is organizing them and they're something a majority of people would be interested in.
All of the above apply just for the YC founders list - you are still free to email your own batch, and we recommend you start there for most questions.
Finally, thanks for making the YC list awesome. It is a really valuable resource and the guidelines above are meant to keep it that way.

title: Black Clouds on the Horizon
transcript:
P
Lycfounders] black clouds on the horizon » YCFounders x
Paul Graham pg@ycombinator.com via googlegroups.com
to ycfounders ×
Unsubscribe
Jessica and I had dinner recently with a prominent investor. He
seemed sure the bad performance of the Facebook PO will hurt the
funding market for earlier stage startups. But no one knows yet
how much. Possibly only a little. Possibly a lot, if it becomes a
vicious circle.
What does this mean for you? If it means new startups raise their
first money on worse terms than they would have a few months ago,
that's not the end of the world, because by historical standards
valuations had been high. Airbnb and Dropbox prove you can raise
money at a fraction of recent valuations and do just fine. What I
do worry about is (a) it may be harder to raise money at all,
regardless of price and (b) that companies that previously raised
money at high valuations will now face "down rounds," which can be
damaging.
What to do?
If you haven't raised money yet, lower your expectations for
fundraising. How much should you lower them? We don't know yet
how hard it will be to raise money or what will happen to valuations
for those who do. Which means it's more important than ever to be
flexible about the valuation you expect and the amount you want to
raise (which, odd as it may seem, are connected). First talk to
investors about whether they want to invest at all, then negotiate
price.

title: Black Clouds on the Horizon (2 of 2)
transcript:
If you raised money in an equity round at a high valuation, you may
find that if you need money you can only get it at a lower one.
Which is bad, because "down rounds" not only dilute you horribly,
but make you seem and perhaps even feel like damaged goods.
The best solution is not to need money. The less you need investor
money, (a) the more investors like you, in all markets, and (b) the
less you're harmed by bad markets.
I often tell startups after raising money that they should act as
if it's the last they're ever going to get. In the past that has
been a useful heuristic, because doing that is the best way to
ensure it's easy to raise more. But if the funding market tanks,
it's going to be more than a heuristic.
The startups that really get hosed are going to be the ones that
have easy money built into the structure of their company: the ones
that raise a lot on easy terms, and are then led thereby to spend
a lot, and to pay little attention to profitability. That kind of
startup gets destroyed when markets tighten up. So don't be that
startup. If you've raised a lot, don't spend it; not merely for
the obvious reason that you'll run out faster, but because it will
turn you into the wrong sort of company to thrive in bad times.
—-Pg
[After reading this, Sam wanted to add two points:
I'd add a suggestion to companies that if they're planning to raise
money in the next year, they consider doing it now (except for
companies in the current batch). Things haven't gotten way worse
yet but they could get a LOT worse quickly.
Also, if companies are doing down rounds, they should talk to us.
I believe down rounds should generally be a big reset of the cap
table--they cause a huge amount of pain either as a small down round
or a big down round, and you may as well use it to the company's
advantage.J

title: Handling Technical Due Diligence with VCs
transcript:
Handling technical due diligence with VCs

Paul Graham <cryptograham@gmail.com> Mon, Sep 7, 2009 at 6:20 PM
Reply-To: cryptograham@gmail.com
To: Slava Akhmechet <coffeemug@gmail.com>
Cc: s2009 founders <s2009founders@googlegroups.com>

If the "experts" are talking out of their asses, you ought
to be able to turn the tables on them by asking questions
like "What about them seems similar to us?"

On Mon, Sep 7, 2009 at 9:17 PM, Trevor Blackwell <tlb@tlb.org> wrote:

"Isn't [first related thing that comes to mind] doing the same thing?"
is a great interviewing trick. Ask a random question, then whatever
area they seem most defensive about you drill down into. You don't
have to know anything about the topic to do it, and you learn a lot
from the way people handle it.

If you're on the receiving end and you know what you're talking
about, then answer. But if you don't, you can only dig yourself a hole
by engaging. The best answer is to say, confidently, "I don't know
what they're doing. I don't think it can be very similar, or I'd know
about it. But I'll check them out tonight and email everyone about it."

That email is a perfect pretext to be on the VC's radar screen the
next day. Start the email with something like:

X asked in the meeting if Y was already doing what we're doing.
They're not (see detailed explanation below). Were there any other
issues? Otherwise, what's the next step towards closing?

On Sep 7, 2009, at 20:04, Slava Akhmechet wrote:

We recently had a somewhat unpleasant technical due diligence
experience. There were a couple of technical experts at the meeting,
and a partner. We explained our technology, and the experts said a
number of things along the lines of "this isn't new, company X has
done this before and failed", "company Y already does what you're
doing with simpler technology", etc. We knew nothing about X and Y.
When we got home and checked, it turned out that these companies have
absolutely nothing in common with what we're doing (technically, and
in terms of the value proposition) - this is why we didn't know about
them.

As a result, the experts looked good in front of the partner, and we
looked like we don't know what we're doing. It's usually very easy for
the experts to set this situation up - they just have to mention an
unrelated technology. The odds are good we won't know about it because
it's unrelated to what we're doing, which means we can't reason about
it.

Could someone suggest how to handle this situation? How could one
counter these objections at a meeting? Also, should we e-mail the
partner after the meeting and counter the objections after we do the
research?

- Slava (RethinkDB)

title: The Airbnb Craigslist Secret Weapon
transcript:
The Airbnb Story
founders were still doing everything they could to
generate growth. Many of the company's new list-
ings and users were coming from PR and word of
mouth, as well as from the frequent trips Gebbia and
Chesky would take around big conventions to try to
"turn on" new markets with events, host meet-ups,
and other guerilla-marketing tactics.
But they had another secret weapon in Blechar-
czyk, who was making clever use of new tools and
technologies available to implement several "growth
hacks." He'd created technology to interface with
Google's AdWords advertising service, for example,
to allow Airbnb to more efficiently target potential
users in specific cities. He also cooked up a clever
tool by building a back door into Craigslist. In 2009,
Craigslist was one of the few sites that had massive
scale—it had amassed tens of millions of users—yet
it was easily penetrable by marketers and clever
entrepreneurs looking to tap in. Blecharczyk created
a one-click integration tool whereby Airbnb users
could click a button embedded in an e-mail sent to
them and instantly rebroadcast their listings on
Craigslist. Their listing would be viewable by
Craigslist's millions of viewers, but the tool brought
the actual bookings back to Airbnb. Many in the
engineering community tipped their hats to Airbnb
for the sheer ingenuity of the feat, calling it a "re-
markable integration"—especially since Craigslist
didn't have a public API, or application program-
ming interface, an official set of rules and guidelines
for one piece of software to work with another.
"This was something that frankly nobody else had,"
Blecharczyk says. "But because of our know-how,
we were able to do it." They experimented with
Craigslist in ways that drew criticism, too, at one
point hiring contractors who set up automated tar-
geted e-mails to Craigslist users who'd listed their
homes on the site for rent, soliciting them to try
Airbnb instead. (The company says leveraging
Craigslist was common back in those days but it
wasn't aware the contractors were engaging in the
spamming, which didn't result in meaningful busi-
ness, and that when they found out they shut it
down.) And, of course, when they went to South by
Southwest back in 2008, they had lured their first
host, Tiendung Le, off of Craigslist to host Chesky
on AirBed & Breakfast instead.
The growth hacks became less meaningful over
time, as real momentum grew. But it's hard to over-
estimate the significance of the ability to find these
"free ways to grow," as Blecharczyk calls them; had
the founders not implemented them, the company
might not have mushroomed the way it did.
